title: Thyroid disease: assessment and management
authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
journal: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NICE guideline NG145, published 20 November 2019, last updated 12 October 2023
result: Offer levothyroxine first-line for primary hypothyroidism; do not routinely offer liothyronine alone or with levothyroxine, because there is not enough evidence of benefit over monotherapy and its long-term adverse effects are uncertain; do not offer natural thyroid extract. Start 1.6 µg/kg/day under 65 without cardiovascular disease, 25 to 50 µg/day with titration at 65 or over or with cardiovascular disease; aim for TSH within the reference range and avoid doses causing TSH suppression or thyrotoxicosis. In subclinical hypothyroidism consider levothyroxine when TSH is 10 mIU/l or higher on 2 occasions 3 months apart, and a 6-month trial for adults under 65 with TSH above the reference range but below 10 on 2 occasions and symptoms, stopping if symptoms persist once TSH is in range. The rationale states that there was little evidence on treating subclinical hypothyroidism, mostly in older adults; that TSH 5 to 10 mIU/l may return to the reference range without treatment in about half of people; that for TSH below 10 the committee judged, based on its experience, the balance most favourable under 65; and that over 65 improvement is less likely and harms from TSH suppression, such as atrial fibrillation, greater. Evidence from 7 trials suggested no important benefit of levothyroxine with liothyronine.
